title: KV Cache architecture & eviction troubleshoot with Luxor Security
next_steps: Redwood to run a KV-cache instrumentation benchmark on Luxor sample workload
Luxor to share example long-context prompt set and traffic profile
Schedule follow-up to review benchmark results and security docs (possible week of 2026-03-16)
Share dedicated deployment pricing and VPC checklist
action_items: Jordan Lee: Send KV cache instrumentation guide and instrumentation script (due: 2026-03-06)
Priya Natarajan: Run memory/eviction simulation with Luxor sample set and share trace logs (due: 2026-03-12)
Ben Torres: Share sample traffic histogram and token distribution (due: 2026-03-08)
summary: Deep-dive on persistent KV cache behavior; customer seeing frequent evictions and paging with long-context sessions and prefix reuse. SE and SRE walked through architecture, metrics to collect, likely root causes (per-shard LRU, small cache slab sizes, tokenization mismatch, aggressive TTLs), and next steps to run targeted benchmarks and instrumentation. Security/VPC and on-prem constraints discussed briefly; Luxor wants bench results before pilot decision.
topics: Quantization impact on memory and kv sizes
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-05 15:00 UTC | Duration: 58m | Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Marco (Redwood SRE) -- Aisha, Ben, Marta, Daniel (Luxor).

Summary (auto): Luxor reports high rate of KV cache evictions during sustained long-context sessions; contexts up to 120k tokens occasionally; prefix reuse across customers causing cache churn; observed latency spikes during paging. SE walked through eviction policies, sharding, instrumentation to capture per-key TTL/last-access, and recommended transient fixes (increase slab sizes, hotspot pinning) plus long-term (adaptive tenant-aware sharding, persistent warmstores).

[00:00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, do we have Aisha and Ben there?
[00:00:05] Aisha: yes hi sorry for the slight delay, can hear you fine
[00:00:10] Ben: here as well, Marta and Daniel on mute - we got the session notes you sent, excited to dig in
[00:00:18] Jordan: great, quick agenda - Priya will walk through kv cache internals, Marco will talk instrumentation and SLOs, then we'll troubleshoot the eviction cases you sent. then next steps
[00:00:29] Priya: cool thanks - i'll start with a quick topo of Redwood's KV cache implementation as it relates to serving runtime. high-level it's a sharded LRU-style cache keyed by (model, session/prefix id, token position) — we keep dense caches per-GPU or per-worker process, not a single global store. that gives lower latency but means per-shard capacity matters
[00:00:50] Marta: question - when you say per-worker, is that per-GPU or per-container? in our setup we saw evictions even when cluster-level memory looked fine
[00:00:58] Priya: good question. it's per-GPU in the Hosted runtime, and in Dedicated it's per-worker process pinned to a GPU. so your cluster memory can be underutilized but individual GPU slabs can be full which causes local evictions
[00:01:14] Ben: that lines up with what we saw - aggregate GPU memory usage looked fine but eviction counters on the worker were high.
[00:01:22] Priya: right, and two other things that commonly bite teams: tokenization mismatch (different token counts between client-side and server-side leads to unexpected prefix reuse patterns), and quantization altering KV sizes (8-bit vs 4-bit weight packs can change working set)
[00:01:38] Aisha: we are using a custom tokenizer upstream for anonymization, could that be a cause? we also do prefix rewriting at the application layer
[00:01:46] Priya: yes, custom tokenizers can cause the same logical prefix to be represented differently resulting in duplicate entries rather than reuse, which increases pressure; prefix rewriting also can either improve reuse or break it depending on canonicalization
[00:01:58] Jordan: Marco can you walk through the metrics we should collect to root cause?
[00:02:02] Marco: sure. minimum list: per-shard cache capacity, per-shard eviction count over time, per-key last-access timestamps, distribution of key sizes (kv bytes), percent of cache entries that are single-session vs cross-session, pagefaults/paging counts if using NVMe backing, and request-level traces with trace_id mapping to cache hits/misses
[00:02:24] Marta: we have some traces but not per-key sizes, how invasive is the instrumentation?
[00:02:29] Marco: we can add lightweight probes - sample 1% of keys to record size and last-access, and add counters for miss/hit/miss_reason. the overhead is small but you do need to enable trace-level logging for short windows to avoid log flood
[00:02:43] Ben: when you say miss_reason, what are the typical kinds? eviction, not-found, token-mismatch?
[00:02:49] Priya: miss_reason taxonomy: cold-miss (never cached), eviction (used to exist but removed), mismatch (different canonical key), expired (TTL), and spill/paging (moved to secondary storage and not in fast slab)
[00:02:59] Daniel: we definitely saw spikes correlated with our nightly long-run job that stitches large histories for e-discovery, lots of long context requests
[00:03:05] Priya: long-contexts are the classic stressor because KV cache size scales roughly linear with prefix length depending on model's kv per token. couple of quick math notes: for decoder-only models, each cached kv entry per token is sized by head/hidden dims and quantization; so a 120k token session creates substantial working set. if you have many concurrent long sessions you'll see eviction churn
[00:03:29] Aisha: our worst-case is about 40 concurrent sessions with mean context 60k, peak 120k, and lots of prefix reuse across sessions since similar queries are stitched with different user IDs
[00:03:40] Priya: ok that explains it. configurations that help: increase per-GPU slab size, enable prefix pinning for hot prefixes, and introduce tenant-aware sharding so identical prefixes across sessions keep a single hot entry instead of duplicates across shards
[00:03:56] Ben: you mentioned paging — is that NVMe backing? we're on Dedicated now and considering Private with NVMe local SSDs for persistent KV
[00:04:04] Marco: yes we support optional NVMe backing for cold pages; when working set exceeds slab we spill to NVMe. but paging has latency cost - you can see 20-200ms spikes while fetching spilled pages depending on IO stack. not ideal for 99th percentile latency sensitive apps
[00:04:18] Priya: additionally, eviction/paging interplay: if eviction policy is simple LRU across shards, you can thrash pages between slab and NVMe. adaptive policies like frequency-aware LRU (LFU or TinyLFU) help avoid thrash for reused prefixes
[00:04:33] Marta: how do you handle prefix reuse across sessions — is there a global canonicalization?
[00:04:37] Priya: we have canonicalization hooks - you can provide a prefix hash that maps identical content to the same canonical key; otherwise we default to session-scoped keys. so app-level canonicalization (or Redwood's prefix normalization layer) is recommended when many sessions share content
[00:04:51] Ben: we have canonicalization but it's not applied consistently due to anonymization earlier in the pipeline - that may be the source of duplicates
[00:04:58] Aisha: ok so action: Ben will pull a sample of canonicalization mismatches and send them over
[00:05:05] Jordan: quick interruption - any security concerns with canonical keys being shared across tenants?
[00:05:11] Marco: good point. Redwood supports tenant-aware ACLs; canonical keys can be scoped with tenant id or flagged as cross-tenant if explicitly allowed. for Luxor you'd likely keep tenant scoping and only canonicalize within tenant to be safe
[00:05:24] Daniel: we need audit logs for any cross-tenant cache promotions - compliance requires provable separation
[00:05:29] Priya: yes audit logs and KMS integration are available, we'll include the security checklist in the follow-up docs
[00:05:36] Jordan: ok back to eviction - are there known bugs or setups that cause unusual rapid eviction?
[00:05:42] Priya: a few: small STABLE slab sizes combined with a bursty token distribution; aggressive TTLs intended for privacy but too short; tokenization-induced duplication; and shard imbalance when routing doesn't consider prefix affinity leading to hot keys spread across many shards rather than localized
[00:06:00] Ben: we saw some shards with 90% occupancy and others at 30% - is that a routing issue?
[00:06:05] Marco: likely yes - if routing hashes to GPU purely by session id but prefixes are similar across sessions you'll get uneven hotspots. sticky routing or consistent hashing with affinity buckets helps. also consider hot-key pinning to a single shard to avoid duplicates
[00:06:20] Priya: on the runtime side, bumping the per-shard capacity and enabling hotspot pinning are low-risk. medium-term: implement adaptive eviction like TinyLFU and tenant-aware sharding; long-term: coordinated global cache or a fast global index (but that's more complex)
[00:06:36] Aisha: what's the downside to just increasing slab sizes? we have spare GPU memory in some nodes
[00:06:42] Priya: scaling slab sizes reduces eviction but increases memory footprint per-worker and can reduce concurrency if you pin more to a GPU. also doesn't fix duplication due to poor canonicalization. there's a cost tradeoff and capacity planning consideration
[00:06:55] Ben: what about batching changes? we saw latency drop with larger micro-batches but cache pressure changed too
[00:07:01] Priya: batching interacts because you amortize compute but increase transient working set while the batch is processed. larger batches can increase peak kv working set leading to temporary evictions if slabs are tight. tuning batching and slab sizes together is important
[00:07:15] Marta: quantization - we recently moved to 4-bit and saw smaller model sizes; does that change cache sizes?
[00:07:20] Priya: yes quantization can reduce KV entry sizes particularly if we store compressed representations; but some 4-bit kernels change how kv is stored in memory and can increase transient unpacked size. measure after conversion. sometimes 4-bit gives net reduction in static memory but transient buffers can spike
[00:07:35] Marco: note also that different library backends (cuBLAS vs custom kernels) have different memory layouts so kv bytes per token vary by backend; record backend as part of instrumentation
[00:07:46] Jordan: can we look at one of the traces Luxor shared? Ben, you sent a few - Priya and Marco had pre-read notes
[00:07:52] Ben: yes i uploaded three traces to the shared folder, trace id lux-trace-042, -043, -044. the one with 300ms tail spikes is lux-trace-043
[00:08:00] Priya: opening trace 043 — i can see repeated cache misses for the same logical prefix across different worker ids; miss_reason tagged as not-found followed by eviction fill. looks like duplicate entries across shards
[00:08:12] Marco: and there are NVMe read ops around those times. so sequence: request comes in, misses local slab, issues read from NVMe (paging), while read inflight worker evicts other entries to make room, then page returns and gets added, causing thrash
[00:08:26] Aisha: ouch. can we avoid that pattern without buying more NVMe?
[00:08:30] Priya: yes - pin hot prefixes to memory (hot-key pinning), increase slab to avoid paging, or change eviction to avoid evicting recently-paged items. also reduce duplicates via canonicalization so the same prefix isn't loaded multiple times into different slabs
[00:08:45] Ben: is there a config toggle for eviction policy?
[00:08:48] Marco: currently we expose basic policy toggles: LRU, LFU-ish heuristics, and TTL settings. TinyLFU is in our backlog and can be fast-tracked for pilots. we can also implement a 'do-not-evict' list for pinned prefixes
[00:09:00] Priya: operationally for your pilot we can enable 'pin hot prefixes' and raise slab to see improvement quickly; then run longer-term simulation for adaptive sharding
[00:09:09] Jordan: timeline wise, we can run a targeted bench next week if you share traffic profile and sample prompts
[00:09:15] Ben: yes we'll share that by monday
[00:09:18] Marta: one more question on long-context: do you stream KV progressively or load the whole context?
[00:09:23] Priya: we progressively materialize KV as tokens are requested; we don't pre-load entire 120k unless request demands it. however some workloads explicitly request full-context forward pass for scoring which triggers large working sets
[00:09:36] Aisha: for our e-discovery scoring we do full history scoring which likely forces loads. can we do scoring in chunks?
[00:09:41] Priya: yes chunked scoring is a mitigation; Redwood runtime supports incremental scoring where you page in windows and merge logits — lower peak memory but trading some compute overhead and complexity
[00:09:55] Daniel: curious about metrics - what SLOs should we set so we can detect thrash before customers notice?
[00:10:01] Marco: guardrails: per-shard eviction rate threshold (e.g., > 10 evictions/min sustained), NVMe read latency percentiles (p99 > 50ms), cache duplication ratio (unique logical prefixes vs cache entries > 1.2), and request-level cache hit ratio drop below baseline. set alerts on these
[00:10:18] Ben: how do we compute duplication ratio?
[00:10:21] Marco: you need a canonical id per logical prefix - count unique logical ids and compare with total cache keys. this requires enabling a canonicalization hash in instrumentation
[00:10:30] Priya: also trace correlation is important - map request id to cache ops so you can see end-to-end latency impact of misses/paging
[00:10:37] Jordan: we're about 10 minutes in; want to make sure we cover on-prem/VPC notes briefly
[00:10:42] Priya: for Private on-prem deployments the architecture is similar but you control NVMe & network stack. common on-prem pitfalls: noisy neighbors on shared NVMe, slow IO scheduler config, and using non-dedicated GPUs for serving. Redwood's private package includes recommended kernel settings and a deployment checklist
[00:10:58] Marta: our infra folks are worried about auditability and encryption for spilled pages
[00:11:03] Marco: spilled pages can be encrypted at rest using customer KMS; Redwood supports per-customer KMS keys and HSM integration for enterprise. audit logs for page reads/writes are available and can be shipped to your SIEM
[00:11:15] Aisha: ok good. one more specific - TTLs. we put a 5 min TTL on some cached entries for PHI reasons. could that be causing churn?
[00:11:22] Priya: yes very aggressive TTL increases churn; shorter TTLs increase fill rate. if compliance forces short TTLs consider ephemeral caching with pinning for hot prefixes and more conservative TTLs for others. document the compliance requirement and we'll design a hybrid policy
[00:11:36] Ben: can we do a small experiment: lower number of concurrent long-context sessions and see effect?
[00:11:40] Priya: yes priory to bench, run a controlled experiment reducing concurrency and enabling canonicalization. we expect eviction rates to drop significantly if duplicates are removed
[00:11:50] Jordan: ok let's capture concrete next steps now
[00:11:53] Priya: action - we will run a simulation with Luxor sample set. we need: sample prompts, tokenization mapping, traffic histogram, and traces. we'll instrument per-shard evictions and a 1% sample of key-sizes.
[00:12:05] Ben: noted, we'll provide by monday.
[00:12:09] Marco: i'll prepare a config patch for pinning hot prefixes and a recommended slab increase for your cluster size; we can push as trial on dedicated nodes for a few hours and monitor
[00:12:20] Marta: what's the risk of pinning causing memory blowouts?
[00:12:23] Priya: we cap pinned memory budget and have fail-open behavior - if pin budget exceeded we fallback to normal eviction; we'll monitor alerts to avoid surprise OOMs
[00:12:34] Aisha: during the pre-read you noted some anomalies with token counts - can you expand?
[00:12:38] Priya: sure - in some traces client-side token counts were 10-15% different from server-side counts — caused by whitespace normalization and the anonymizer. that leads to logically identical prefixes hashing differently and creates duplicates. fix at source or normalize at ingress
[00:12:56] Ben: we'll look at anonymizer output and add a normalization step.
[00:13:01] Jordan: zooming out - if we implement these mitigations how quickly do we expect 99th p latency to improve?
[00:13:06] Priya: early wins (pinning + slab bump + canonicalization) can reduce p99 spikes caused by paging within hours of deployment; measurable p99 improvement should surface in a day once warmed. bigger changes like adaptive sharding take weeks
[00:13:18] Daniel: do you have reference numbers from other customers?
[00:13:21] Priya: roughly for similar profiles we've seen p99 tail drop from ~300-400ms down to 60-100ms after enabling pinning and removing duplicates; your mileage depends on concurrency and working set size
[00:13:33] Ben: great. any notes on cost impact? larger slabs and pinned memory increases cost per GPU?
[00:13:38] Marco: yes cost rises with reserved memory footprint; we'll estimate tradeoffs in the follow-up pricing doc. Dedicated reserved capacity pricing factors in baseline slab sizes; we'll include delta for your config
[00:13:49] Jordan: quick check - any compliance blockers for enabling instrumentation and traces?
[00:13:54] Marco: traces can be redacted for PHI; we support token-level redaction and will sign an NDA for any deeper logs. persistent logs are optional and can be retained in your VPC only for Private deployments
[00:14:07] Aisha: good. let's talk about a concrete bench run - what do you need?
[00:14:11] Priya: we need a representative sample: 1) 2000 sample prompts covering prefix reuse, 2) tokenization mapping for those prompts, 3) concurrency profile and session durations, 4) goal SLOs for p50/p95/p99 and acceptable cost uplift
[00:14:26] Ben: we can put that together.
[00:14:29] Priya: timeline: we can run microbench in 24-48 hours after receiving data and share results and traces; full sim across many nodes may take longer
[00:14:36] Jordan: ok moving to some lower-level clarifications — eviction policy details and config flags (Priya)?
[00:14:41] Priya: current tunables: per-shard capacity bytes, eviction_policy (LRU|LFU_sim), TTL default, pin_budget_bytes, nvme_spill_threshold, canonicalization_hook_enabled. example recommended starting config for your workload: increase per-shard capacity by 30%, set pin_budget to 10% of slab, enable canonicalization_hook, set nvme_spill_threshold to 85% (so we try to avoid spill until higher pressure)
[00:15:03] Marta: will raising spill threshold cause OOMs on GPU?
[00:15:07] Marco: spill threshold is percentage of slab usage that triggers NVMe spill; combined with slab increase it's safe but we must monitor GPU free memory. we'll set conservative alarms
[00:15:18] Ben: any one-off clever hacks? like keeping a small global hot-index in shared mem?
[00:15:22] Priya: yes some customers implement a small global index that points to the responsible shard and reduces duplicates; Redwood has an experimental fast index we can enable for pilots but it's considered beta
[00:15:34] Aisha: i'd prefer conservative production-grade fixes first then beta later
[00:15:38] Priya: understood. we'll go staged: pin + canonicalization + slab bump, then run simulation, then evaluate beta index if still needed
[00:15:47] Jordan: we're halfway through; any other infra questions?
[00:15:50] Marta: what about monitoring visualization - can we get dashboards?
[00:15:53] Marco: yes we'll share Grafana dashboards with panels for per-shard occupancy, eviction rate, NVMe ops, duplication ratio, and request-level hit/miss latency waterfall
[00:16:03] Ben: will that integrate with our Prometheus?
[00:16:05] Marco: yes we expose Prom metrics; we'll provide scrape configs and dashboards templates
[00:16:11] Aisha: about prefix reuse - can you run an analysis to show which prefixes are hot and duplicated across sessions?
[00:16:17] Priya: yes with sample prompts we can run a hot-prefix analysis and produce a heatmap of duplication across sessions
[00:16:23] Ben: ok sending samples monday
[00:16:26] Priya: one more note on tokenization: if you can share both raw and anonymized versions we can instrument to see mapping and compute canonicalization hit rate
[00:16:35] Jordan: wrapping to timeline - we agreed Redwood runs an instrumentation bench, Luxor provides samples and traffic histogram, Redwood shares config patch and dashboards, then reconvene week of 3/16. action items on the doc
[00:16:49] Daniel: sounds good. quick last question - persistence on NVMe: is it encrypted and what KMS options?
[00:16:55] Marco: yes encrypted at rest using customer-managed KMS (AWS KMS, cloud HSM, or on-prem HSM for Private). we'll include a slide in follow-up docs
[00:17:04] Aisha: thanks everyone, we'll loop in infra and legal post-call for the security checklist
[00:17:10] Jordan: thanks, we'll send notes and next steps shortly.
[00:17:14] [00:17:14] End of structured discussion; remaining time used for troubleshooting trace 044 and Q&A (unstructured).

[00:17:15] [00:20:00] Priya: looking at trace 044 - this one shows canonicalization inconsistencies; same semantic prompt hashed to different keys because anonymizer replaced tokens in different orders
[00:20:22] Ben: yeah that was a bug we had in anonymizer pipeline - we'll patch it
[00:21:02] Priya: after patch, expected duplication ratio should drop, which will show up quickly in eviction counters
[00:21:20] Marco: small thing to watch for - when you patch anonymizer you might change token alignment; ensure downstream components handle re-synced offsets
[00:22:10] Marta: noted. also want to highlight that some of our scoring jobs are less latency sensitive and could be moved to batch offline scoring to reduce pressure
[00:22:20] Priya: yep that's a valid trade-off, offload large scoring to batch or run in a separate capacity tier that has larger slabs and different eviction policies
[00:23:00] Ben: curious - any general heuristics for when to choose Dedicated vs Private for this workload?
[00:23:06] Jordan: Dedicated is typically faster to pilot and gives reserved GPU pools with Redwood-managed infra; Private gives full network control, KMS in your VPC, and more control over NVMe and deployment configs but takes longer to onboard
[00:23:20] Daniel: ok thanks.
[00:23:35] [00:30:00] Priya: quick note - we'll include a small script that replays sample traffic against a staging cluster to reproduce eviction patterns; it's non-invasive and we can run with you.
[00:30:20] Ben: thanks, that will help.
[00:31:00] [00:40:00] Jordan: any blockers on legal side for sharing traces?
[00:40:10] Aisha: legal wants a redaction confirmation - we need Redwood to attest that traces will be redacted or processed in our VPC only for Private, or with strict NDA for Hosted/Dedicated logs
[00:40:24] Marco: we'll provide a redaction checklist and can sign an NDA; for Hosted we can also provide hashed-only traces with no PHI
[00:40:36] Aisha: good.
[00:41:00] [00:50:00] (Unstructured troubleshooting continues - Priya walks through a micro trace, Marco highlights nvme IO spikes, Ben commits to sample pushes)

[00:50:30] Jordan: last wrap - i'll compile the notes and action items and share the recording and slides. thanks everyone
[00:50:40] Aisha: appreciate the time, good session
[00:50:45] Ben: thanks all
[00:50:48] Meeting end.

Note: transcription contains minor auto-transcription errors (names/acronyms) - please refer to shared artifact trace ids and uploaded logs for definitive values.
